title: ND DMA: two paddings, a three-loop selection and a transpose
surface: gm_to_ub_nd_dma(dst, src, loop_src_strides, loop_dst_strides, loop_sizes, loop_left_pad=, loop_right_pad=, config_left_pad=, config_right_pad=, constant_value=, nearest_value_mode=, fence=) and the gm_to_ub_nd_dma_transpose shorthand
study_for: Loop 0 is the innermost one, and every stride counts elements. The three lists are source strides, destination strides and iteration counts, in that loop order, which is why the row-selection transfer reads `[1, 2*COLS, 8*COLS]`, `[1, 32, 128]`, `[32, 4, 2]` -- 32 contiguous columns, then four rows two apart, then two blocks eight rows apart, giving rows 0, 2, ... 14 of `x[:, :32]`. Reading those three lists outside-in is the mistake that produces a plausible transfer of the wrong elements.

Two spellings of the same padding, and what picks between them. `loop_left_pad=[3, 2]` pads per loop -- three on the inner, two on the outer -- while `config_left_pad=8` is the default every loop takes when no per-loop list is given; the printer emits them into the same `NdLoops` field. The BF16 transfer uses the config form because all its loops want the same eight elements a side.

What the padded positions are filled with. `constant_value=-1.5` writes a literal, and `nearest_value_mode=True` repeats the nearest real element of that loop instead -- edge replication, which the reference states independently as `F.pad(..., mode='replicate')`. The two cases pad the same window both ways in one launch, so the difference between them is visible side by side rather than across runs.

`fence` decides what closes the transfer. The default `all` ends it with `pipe_barrier(PIPE_ALL)`; the BF16 transfer passes `fence='mte2'` instead, which scopes the wait to the transfer pipe. It is the one attribute here that changes the synchronisation rather than the data, so a copy of this line into a kernel whose next reader is not on MTE2 is a copy of the wrong thing.

The transpose is sugar, not a separate path. `gm_to_ub_nd_dma_transpose(ub_t, x[0:16, 0:32])` builds the same ND loops with the rows walking innermost; the reference is `x[:16, :32].T.contiguous()`. Comparing the whole 32x16 destination is what makes that a statement about every element rather than about the shape.
do_not_copy_when: Your destination tile is not the one these transfers were sized for. Each UB tensor here is declared at the exact padded destination shape, and the pads are counted in elements of that shape. A different width changes where the border lands and the numbers in the three lists stop describing it.

You want the BF16 path's rounding checked. Nothing here rounds: the transfer copies BF16 bytes and pads them with a value that is exact in BF16. The reference widens to FP32 only so `F.pad` can take the value, then narrows back -- a passing run says the transfer preserved bytes, not that any conversion is right.
You are after cross-core ordering. One vector participant owns every write here, so `fence` is about pipes inside a core and nothing in this folder exercises two cores touching the same destination.
